topics.title: § 4.1.1 — Pre-Hearing Notice & Parties (pp. 155–162)
topics.description: Classes 11–12: Block (syllabus calls it Bloch), fair charge notice, laches, initiation and intervention

entries.title: Notice rights and preparation for defense
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 155–159
entries.summary: Administrative notice must reach affected party by reasonably calculated means and describe charges sufficiently for meaningful defense.
entries.laymanExplanation: Administrative notice must reach affected party by reasonably calculated means and describe charges sufficiently for meaningful defense.
entries.legalExplanation: APA § 554(b) requires notice of time/place/nature, legal authority, and facts/law asserted; the due process delivery test in Dusenbery differs from the detailed charging requirement analyzed in Block.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish actual receipt, delivery attempts, specificity, and loss of possible alibi defense.
entries.examTrap: Do not use criminal indictment specificity as a universal rule for agency licensing.

entries.title: Block v. Ambach, 537 N.E.2d 181 (N.Y. 1989)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 155–157
entries.summary: No. Broad periods adequately described ongoing conduct and the nature of misconduct so he could present a meaningful defense.
entries.laymanExplanation: No. Broad periods adequately described ongoing conduct and the nature of misconduct so he could present a meaningful defense.
entries.legalExplanation: Must administrative license-revocation charges allege exact dates to give procedural due process? Due process requires reasonable specificity in context; the licensee fully contested charges and did not seek event-specific alibis, while criminal charging rules protect different concerns.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: New York charged psychiatrist Ackerman with sexual misconduct with patients during long time ranges; he denied sexual conduct and even patient relationship, but argued that no specific misconduct dates deprived him of an alibi.
entries.issue: Must administrative license-revocation charges allege exact dates to give procedural due process?
entries.holding: No. Broad periods adequately described ongoing conduct and the nature of misconduct so he could present a meaningful defense.
entries.reasoning: Due process requires reasonable specificity in context; the licensee fully contested charges and did not seek event-specific alibis, while criminal charging rules protect different concerns.
entries.rule: The charge must be sufficiently specific in circumstances to apprise respondent of allegations and permit preparation of adequate defense.
entries.examApplication: Compare the discrete theft allegations in Wolfe; ask whether lack of dates materially prevents a defense.
entries.examTrap: Professor syllabus spells Bloch; uploaded casebook prints Block. Both refer to the case in this source.

entries.title: Continuous misconduct and discrete incidents
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 156–160
entries.summary: General time periods may describe continuous conduct, but discrete incidents may require particular dates and locations for an alibi.
entries.laymanExplanation: General time periods may describe continuous conduct, but discrete incidents may require particular dates and locations for an alibi.
entries.legalExplanation: Block did not demand date-by-date notice for repeated treatment-related misconduct; Wolfe found unfairness in a vague two-year frame for three or four specific thefts.
entries.examApplication: Find nature of violations, factual disputes, and concrete defense impairment.

entries.title: Wolfe v. Kelly, 911 N.Y.S.2d 362 (App. Div. 2010)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 159–160
entries.summary: Two-year time frame without dates or places for several discrete narcotics theft allegations denied due process.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two-year time frame without dates or places for several discrete narcotics theft allegations denied due process.
entries.legalExplanation: Cooperating officer witnesses could not specify details, leaving accused policeman unable to present concrete rebuttal.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Distinguish from Block's continuing misconduct.

entries.title: Dusenbery v. United States, 534 U.S. 161 (2002)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 158–159
entries.summary: Certified mail to a prisoner could be reasonable despite loss inside the prison.
entries.laymanExplanation: Certified mail to a prisoner could be reasonable despite loss inside the prison.
entries.legalExplanation: Reasonably calculated to notify, not guaranteed actual notice, governs forfeiture notice.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Analyze adequacy of attempts, not hindsight receipt.

entries.title: Jones v. Flowers, 547 U.S. 220 (2006)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 158–159
entries.summary: Returned 'unclaimed' certified mail may require practicable additional reasonable steps.
entries.laymanExplanation: Returned 'unclaimed' certified mail may require practicable additional reasonable steps.
entries.legalExplanation: Knowledge of delivery failure changes notice duties.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Contrast absent actual receipt in Dusenbery.

entries.title: Time limits and laches for stale charges
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 157–158
entries.summary: Licensing discipline often has no direct limitation statute; laches generally requires unreasonable delay causing prejudice, though states vary.
entries.laymanExplanation: Licensing discipline often has no direct limitation statute; laches generally requires unreasonable delay causing prejudice, though states vary.
entries.legalExplanation: The text contrasts criminal time limits with civil regulatory discipline and gives examples of missing witnesses, faded memory and agency delay. 28 U.S.C. §§ 2462 and 2401 may supply distinct limits in covered matters.
entries.examApplication: Apply applicable statute first; then show delay and actual prejudice.
entries.examTrap: Do not import criminal limitations without statutory basis.

entries.title: Granek v. Texas State Board of Medical Examiners, 172 S.W.3d 761 (Tex. App. 2005)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 158
entries.summary: Long delay prejudiced defense to one physician charge but not another where allegation was promptly reported.
entries.laymanExplanation: Long delay prejudiced defense to one physician charge but not another where allegation was promptly reported.
entries.legalExplanation: Texas discussion emphasizes prejudice, not the standard two-part laches framework.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Compare evidence preserved contemporaneously.

entries.title: Initiation versus intervention
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 160–162
entries.summary: Private third parties generally cannot compel discretionary agency enforcement absent a statutory right; intervention is becoming a party in an existing hearing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Private third parties generally cannot compel discretionary agency enforcement absent a statutory right; intervention is becoming a party in an existing hearing.
entries.legalExplanation: The private right to initiate enforcement differs from rights of interested persons to participate under APA § 555(b), limited by orderly conduct of agency business.
entries.examApplication: For each party, decide whether case exists yet, an applicable statute grants initiation rights, and whether intervention would help versus burden the agency.

entries.title: Heckler v. Chaney, 470 U.S. 821 (1985)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 160–161
entries.summary: Agency nonenforcement ordinarily falls within its discretion.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency nonenforcement ordinarily falls within its discretion.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook uses FDA nonenforcement in execution-drug context to illustrate lack of compelled private prosecution.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Check specific statutory rights of initiation.

entries.title: United Church of Christ v. FCC, 359 F.2d 994 (D.C. Cir. 1966)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 161
entries.summary: Television viewers could demand license hearing and participate in administrative matter.
entries.laymanExplanation: Television viewers could demand license hearing and participate in administrative matter.
entries.legalExplanation: Book cautions later cases decoupled administrative standing from judicial review standing.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Analyze distinct statutes and policies.

entries.title: Animal Legal Defense Fund v. Vilsack, 237 F. Supp. 3d 15 (2017)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 162
entries.summary: USDA could exercise discretion over interested group intervention but had to analyze adequate representation, delay, scope and help to decision.
entries.laymanExplanation: USDA could exercise discretion over interested group intervention but had to analyze adequate representation, delay, scope and help to decision.
entries.legalExplanation: A conclusory refusal unsupported by relevant agency factors was arbitrary/capricious.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Apply § 555(b) balancing, not automatic judicial standing.

topics.title: § 4.1.2 — Investigation, Subpoenas & Discovery (pp. 163–173)
topics.description: Classes 11–12: investigatory power, Craib, Fourth/Fifth Amendment, privileged material, inspections, p. 172 problem

entries.title: Subpoena authority comes from agency statute
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 163–164
entries.summary: Agencies can compel records or testimony only if their substantive statutes authorize subpoenas/CIDs; APA alone provides no inherent compulsory investigative power.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agencies can compel records or testimony only if their substantive statutes authorize subpoenas/CIDs; APA alone provides no inherent compulsory investigative power.
entries.legalExplanation: APA §§ 555(c),(d), 556(c)(2) describe procedural issues, while enabling laws define powers. Many agency records arrive voluntarily; PRA and OIRA address paper burdens.
entries.examApplication: Identify jurisdiction, enabling statute, kind of investigative demand and whether a hearing has commenced.

entries.title: Craib v. Bulmash, 777 P.2d 1120 (Cal. 1989)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 163–168
entries.summary: No. A lawful, sufficiently specific records subpoena is subject to administrative reasonableness, not criminal probable cause; required regulatory records could be compelled notwithstanding self-incrimination objection.
entries.laymanExplanation: No. A lawful, sufficiently specific records subpoena is subject to administrative reasonableness, not criminal probable cause; required regulatory records could be compelled notwithstanding self-incrimination objection.
entries.legalExplanation: Did wage-record subpoena violate Fourth Amendment warrant requirements or Fifth Amendment self-incrimination? Oklahoma Press approves investigative subpoenas relevant to lawful inquiry without intrusive entry. Shapiro required-records doctrine applies to wage records. Justice Mosk dissented under state constitutional self-incrimination protections and urged immunity.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: California labor commissioner subpoenaed legally required wage records from person employing his sister's caretakers; he refused and asserted Fourth and Fifth Amendment defenses.
entries.issue: Did wage-record subpoena violate Fourth Amendment warrant requirements or Fifth Amendment self-incrimination?
entries.holding: No. A lawful, sufficiently specific records subpoena is subject to administrative reasonableness, not criminal probable cause; required regulatory records could be compelled notwithstanding self-incrimination objection.
entries.reasoning: Oklahoma Press approves investigative subpoenas relevant to lawful inquiry without intrusive entry. Shapiro required-records doctrine applies to wage records. Justice Mosk dissented under state constitutional self-incrimination protections and urged immunity.
entries.rule: Lawful, relevant and sufficiently particular agency records subpoenas can be court-enforced; records required under legitimate regulatory scheme commonly lack Fifth Amendment protection.
entries.examApplication: Separate subpoena, actual search/inspection, testimonial act of producing records and state constitutional dissent.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume all records subpoenas are immune to Fourth Amendment or all individual documents lack privilege.

entries.title: Oklahoma Press subpoena-reasonableness framework
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 164–166
entries.summary: Administrative subpoena ordinarily needs delegated authority, legitimate purpose, relevance, reasonable specificity and nonoppressive breadth, not probable cause of a particular crime.
entries.laymanExplanation: Administrative subpoena ordinarily needs delegated authority, legitimate purpose, relevance, reasonable specificity and nonoppressive breadth, not probable cause of a particular crime.
entries.legalExplanation: Actual forced entry is different from future court-enforced production at agency offices.
entries.examApplication: Check agency jurisdiction, relation of material to investigation and opportunity to challenge before penalties.
entries.examTrap: Do not confuse subpoena issued by agency with warrant allowing forced physical inspection.

entries.title: Oklahoma Press Publishing Co. v. Walling, 327 U.S. 186 (1946)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 164–165
entries.summary: Created broad administrative records-subpoena framework.
entries.laymanExplanation: Created broad administrative records-subpoena framework.
entries.legalExplanation: No agency complaint or criminal probable cause needed for relevant authorized investigation.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Cite for Craib's Fourth Amendment analysis.

entries.title: Marshall v. Barlow's, Inc., 436 U.S. 307 (1978)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 166, 171–172
entries.summary: Nonconsensual inspection of business premises ordinarily requires an administrative warrant.
entries.laymanExplanation: Nonconsensual inspection of business premises ordinarily requires an administrative warrant.
entries.legalExplanation: Warrant may rest on neutral regulatory inspection criteria, not individualized crime suspicion.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Distinguish physical entry from paper subpoena.

entries.title: Required regulatory records and testimonial privilege
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 166–171
entries.summary: Fifth Amendment protects compelled testimonial self-incrimination, but Shapiro required records exception often allows agency to compel business records law requires to be kept.
entries.laymanExplanation: Fifth Amendment protects compelled testimonial self-incrimination, but Shapiro required records exception often allows agency to compel business records law requires to be kept.
entries.legalExplanation: Look separately at prepared contents, compelled act of production, privileged testimony and entity documents.
entries.examApplication: Marchetti excludes certain criminal-targeted reporting; corporate custodians cannot assert personal privilege for entity records; Garrity/use immunity can bar criminal use of compelled testimony.
entries.examTrap: The required-records exception is not a blanket rule for every personally held document.

entries.title: Shapiro v. United States, 335 U.S. 1 (1948)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 166–168
entries.summary: Wage-type regulatory records required by law may be compelled.
entries.laymanExplanation: Wage-type regulatory records required by law may be compelled.
entries.legalExplanation: Craib invokes the exception to Fifth Amendment privilege.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Determine generally regulatory rather than criminal-focused reporting.

entries.title: Marchetti v. United States, 390 U.S. 39 (1968)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 166–167
entries.summary: Gambling records targeting inherently suspect criminal actors may remain privileged.
entries.laymanExplanation: Gambling records targeting inherently suspect criminal actors may remain privileged.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrasts neutral routine regulation with criminal self-reporting.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Check reporting regime's actual purpose and affected group.

entries.title: Defenses to subpoena enforcement
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 168–169
entries.summary: Potential defenses: facial lack of jurisdiction, irrelevance, vagueness, oppressive breadth, bad faith, valid evidentiary privilege or associational burden.
entries.laymanExplanation: Potential defenses: facial lack of jurisdiction, irrelevance, vagueness, oppressive breadth, bad faith, valid evidentiary privilege or associational burden.
entries.legalExplanation: Investigations can be broad but are not unlimited; challengers should show concrete defects.
entries.examApplication: Bad-faith discovery requires preliminary factual showing; federal appellate review of enforcement decisions generally abuse of discretion.
entries.examTrap: Vague objections to 'fishing expeditions' rarely prevail.

entries.title: Major League Baseball v. Crist, 331 F.3d 1177 (11th Cir. 2003)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 168–169
entries.summary: CID unenforceable where state lacked authority over MLB due to federal exemption.
entries.laymanExplanation: CID unenforceable where state lacked authority over MLB due to federal exemption.
entries.legalExplanation: No jurisdiction over subject means no valid related investigation.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Use for authority threshold.

entries.title: United States v. Clarke, 573 U.S. 248 (2014)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 169
entries.summary: Bad faith requires plausible showing before exploring investigators' motives.
entries.laymanExplanation: Bad faith requires plausible showing before exploring investigators' motives.
entries.legalExplanation: Disbelief without facts cannot open broad discovery.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Use for improper-purpose challenges.

entries.title: McLane Co. v. EEOC, 581 U.S. 72 (2017)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 169
entries.summary: Subpoena enforcement reviewed for abuse of discretion on appeal.
entries.laymanExplanation: Subpoena enforcement reviewed for abuse of discretion on appeal.
entries.legalExplanation: Explains deferential posture of enforcing judge's order.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced

entries.title: Administrative Fifth Amendment practical limits
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 169–171
entries.summary: Witness must generally attend and assert privilege to particular answers; adverse civil inference possible; testimonial immunity may permit compulsion while criminal-use restriction applies.
entries.laymanExplanation: Witness must generally attend and assert privilege to particular answers; adverse civil inference possible; testimonial immunity may permit compulsion while criminal-use restriction applies.
entries.legalExplanation: Unlike a criminal defendant, a licensee cannot simply refuse every question without consequences.
entries.examApplication: See Baxter for inferences; Keating for no automatic stay pending criminal case; Garrity/Lefkowitz for compelled statement protection; Braswell for collective entity records.
entries.examTrap: Differentiate administrative penalty use from later criminal evidentiary use.

entries.title: Baxter v. Palmigiano, 425 U.S. 308 (1976)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 170
entries.summary: Silence can support adverse inference in administrative discipline.
entries.laymanExplanation: Silence can support adverse inference in administrative discipline.
entries.legalExplanation: Civil and criminal use of privilege differ.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced

entries.title: Garrity v. New Jersey, 385 U.S. 493 (1967)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 170

entries.title: Braswell v. United States, 487 U.S. 99 (1988)

entries.title: Physical inspections and closely regulated businesses
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 171–172
entries.summary: Routine physical inspections require administrative warrants absent valid exceptions; pervasively regulated industries may be inspected under Burger safeguards.
entries.laymanExplanation: Routine physical inspections require administrative warrants absent valid exceptions; pervasively regulated industries may be inspected under Burger safeguards.
entries.legalExplanation: Search of premises is more intrusive than document production.

entries.title: Administrative discovery is usually by agency rule

topics.title: § 4.1.3 — Alternative Dispute Resolution (pp. 173–175)

entries.title: Negotiation, mediation, arbitration
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 173–174
entries.summary: Negotiation is direct party settlement; mediation uses neutral facilitator without power to decide; arbitration gives the neutral decision authority.
entries.laymanExplanation: Negotiation is direct party settlement; mediation uses neutral facilitator without power to decide; arbitration gives the neutral decision authority.
entries.legalExplanation: ADR may be faster or more flexible than hearing, but important public precedent sometimes needs adjudication.
entries.examApplication: Compare party control, binding effect, public interest, resource cost and flexibility.

entries.title: Administrative Dispute Resolution Act
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 174
entries.summary: Federal APA §§ 556(c)(6)–(8) and 571–583 encourage voluntary agency ADR, while § 572(b) identifies cases where precedent or other considerations make ADR unsuitable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Federal APA §§ 556(c)(6)–(8) and 571–583 encourage voluntary agency ADR, while § 572(b) identifies cases where precedent or other considerations make ADR unsuitable.
entries.legalExplanation: Neither party must be compelled to use it in the framework described.
entries.examApplication: Analyze whether regulators can resolve enforcement while preserving legal clarity and public participation.
